stories.title: Inflation erased the income gain.
stories.dek: New federal figures show inflation absorbed the gain in after-tax income.
stories.script: A new report shows inflation swallowed Americans' income gains. The Bureau of Economic Analysis said Wednesday that after-tax income rose in August. Prices rose too, leaving buying power flat. Annual inflation was three point four percent, above the Fed's two percent goal. The next test: can income start outpacing prices? That's what gives households more room to breathe.
stories.reviewMethod: Editorial accuracy review against BEA release 26-43 and the Federal Reserve definition of its longer-run PCE inflation goal. Aggregate estimates, not every household's experience.
stories.editorialNote: BEA released these August estimates on September 30, 2026, with its annual update. Annual headline PCE inflation was 3.4%; the Federal Reserve goal is 2% over the longer run. After-tax income rose 0.3% in current dollars and was unchanged after inflation; real spending rose 0.6%. No comparison uses unrevised July figures. The closing is a question, not a forecast.

stories.title: Default help moves online
stories.dek: A new federal portal brings default-resolution applications and paperwork online.
stories.script: Borrowers with defaulted federal student loans have a new way to get back on track for repayment, and it's all online. The Treasury and Education departments launched a support center Wednesday that lets borrowers compare rehabilitation and consolidation, upload documents and track progress. Applying is only the start. Borrowers must meet their chosen path's requirements to leave default. Default generally follows about nine months of missed payments and can hurt credit, making a car loan or apartment harder to get.

evidence.headline: U.S. Department of the Treasury and U.S. Department of Education Launch New Defaulted Loans Support Center
evidence.excerpt: September 30, 2026. The U.S. Department of the Treasury (Treasury) and the U.S. Department of Education (ED) announced the launch of the Defaulted Loans Support Center, a new online portal that gives Americans with defaulted federal student loans a simpler way to understand their options, address default, and return to repayment. Now, defaulted borrowers have a centralized portal to: Understand the consequences of default; Compare available paths out of default; Apply online for loan rehabilitation or consolidation; Make a payment on a defaulted loan; and Review repayment plans and loan-discharge options. Borrowers can also complete the loan rehabilitation application online, upload documents, review an estimated payment, electronically sign their agreement, and track progress without leaving StudentAid.gov.

evidence.headline: Student Loan Default and Collections: FAQs
evidence.excerpt: If you don’t make your scheduled loan payments for at least 270 days, your federal student loan goes into default. Loan rehabilitation is a method of getting your federal student loan(s) out of default. You make a certain number of consecutive, on-time payments to ED or the guaranty agency (FFEL borrowers only) under a rehabilitation agreement. You must also sign a Rehabilitation Agreement Letter. If action isn’t taken within 65 days of your loan(s) being placed in default, DRG (on behalf of ED) will report your loan(s) as in default to the four major credit reporting agencies: Equifax, Experian, Innovis, and TransUnion.

evidence.headline: What happens if I default on a federal student loan?
evidence.excerpt: For most federal student loans, you default if you have not made a payment in more than 270 days. If you haven’t made a payment on your federal student loan for at least 270 days (nine months), and you have not entered into an agreement with your lender or servicer to postpone your payments (like deferment or forbearance), you are probably in default. Credit reporting companies are notified, which generally means a lower credit score for you

evidence.headline: Why do I need a credit history?
evidence.excerpt: To make most large purchases, such as homes and cars, people borrow money. Your credit history makes a difference in the cost you pay for the loan. Landlords check your credit to decide whether to rent to you, and whether to ask you for a larger security deposit. When there are negative items on your credit report, like missed payments or high balances, it can be harder or more expensive to do the things you want to do: You could be turned down for a loan or offered a loan with more expensive terms
